The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

As the editors have judged that your manuscript is of interest, but as described below that additional experiments are required before it is published, we would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). First, because many researchers have temporarily lost access to the labs, we will give authors as much time as they need to submit revised manuscripts. We are also offering, if you choose, to post the manuscript to bioRxiv (if it is not already there) along with this decision letter and a formal designation that the manuscript is 'in revision at eLife'. Please let us know if you would like to pursue this option. (If your work is more suitable for medRxiv, you will need to post the preprint yourself, as the mechanisms for us to do so are still in development.)

Summary:

The revised paper presents a better-fitting analysis, and does a more nuanced job in discussing the results, than the original manuscript. However, there are still a few major criticisms that we have for the analysis, detailed below.

Essential revisions:

1) Brain-wide, multiple-comparison corrected tests comparing auditory versus visual decoding are still lacking. The authors have now provided vertex-wise Bayes factors within areas that showed significant decoding in each individual condition. Unfortunately, this is not satisfactory, because these statistics are (1) potentially circular because ROIs were pre-selected based on an analysis of individual conditions, (2) not multiple-comparison corrected, and (3) rely on an arbitrary prior that is not calibrated to the expected effect size. Still, ignoring these issues, the only area that appears to contain vertices with "strong evidence" for a difference in neuro-behavioral decoding is the MOG, which wouldn't really support the claim of "largely distinct networks" supporting audio vs. visual speech representation.

The authors may address these issues, for instance, by

i) presenting additional whole-brain results – e.g. for a direct comparison of auditory and visual classification (in Figure 2) and of perceptual prediction (in Figure 3).

ii) presenting voxel-wise maps of Bayesian evidence values (as in Figure 2—figure supplement 3) for the statistical comparisons shown in Figure 2D, and Figure 3D

iii) in the text included in Figure 2D and 3D making clear what hypotheses correspond to the null hypothesis and to the alternative hypothesis (i.e. auditory = visual, auditory <> visual).

2) As noted before by reviewer 3, the classifiers used in this study do not discriminate between temporal versus spatial dimensions of decoding accuracy. This leaves it unclear whether the reported results are driven by (dis)similarity of spatial patterns of activity (as in fMRI-based MVPA), temporal patterns of activity (e.g., oscillatory "tracking" of the speech signal), or some combination. As these three possibilities could lead to very different interpretations of the data, it seems critical to distinguish between them. For example, the authors write "the encoding of the acoustic speech envelope is seen widespread in the brain, but correct word comprehension correlates only with focal activity in temporal and motor regions," but, as it stands, their results could be partly driven by this non-specific entrainment to the acoustic envelope.

In their response, the authors show that classifier accuracy breaks down when spatial or temporal information is degraded, but it would be more informative to show how these two factors interact. For example, the methods article cited by the authors (Grootswagers, Wardle and Carlson, 2017) shows classification accuracy for successive time bins after stimulus onset (i.e., they train different classifiers for each time bin 0-100 ms, 100-200 ms, etc.). The timing of decoding accuracy in different areas could also help to distinguish between different plausible explanations of the results.

Finally, it is somewhat unclear how spatial and temporal information are combined in the current classifier. Figure 1—figure supplement 2 creates the impression that the time-series for each vertex within a spotlight were simply concatenated. However, this would conflate within-vertex (temporal) and across-vertex (spatial) variance.

3) The concern that the classifier could conceivably index factors influencing "accuracy" rather than the perceived stimulus does not appear to be addressed sufficiently. Indeed, the classifier is referred to as identifying "sensory representations" throughout the manuscript, when it could just as well identify areas involved in any other functions (e.g., attention, motor function) that would contribute to accurate behavioral performance. This limitation should be acknowledged in the manuscript. The authors could consider using the timing of decoding accuracy in different areas to disambiguate these explanations.

The authors state in their response that classifying based on the participant's reported stimulus (rather than response accuracy) could "possibly capture representations not related to speech encoding but relevant for behaviour only (e.g. pre-motor activity). These could be e.g. brain activity that leads to perceptual errors based on intrinsic fluctuations in neural activity in sensory pathways, noise in the decision process favouring one alternative response among four choices, or even noise in the motor system that leads to a wrong button press without having any relation to sensory representations at all."

But, it seems that all of these issues would also effect the accuracy-based classifier as well. Moreover, it seems that intrinsic fluctuations in sensory pathways, or possibly noise in the decision process, are part of what the authors are after. If noise in a sensory pathway can be used to predict particular inaccurate responses, isn't that strong evidence that it encodes behaviorally-relevant sensory representations? For example, intrinsic noise in V1 has been found to predict responses in a simple visual task in non-human primates, with false alarm trials exhibiting noise patterns that are similar to target responses (Seidemann and Geisler, 2018). Showing accurate trial-by-trial decoding of participants' incorrect responses could similarly provide stronger evidence that a certain area contributes to behavior.

claims.claim: Visual speech activates ventral and dorsal visual pathways and bilateral fronto-temporal circuits.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that visual speech activates ventral and dorsal visual pathways and bilateral fronto-temporal circuits (Bernstein and Liebenthal, 2014; Calvert, 1997; Campbell, 2008; Capek et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Some studies have explicitly suggested that auditory regions are also involved in lip reading.
claims.source: Some studies have explicitly suggested that auditory regions are also involved in lip reading (Calvert, 1997; Calvert and Campbell, 2003; Capek et al., 2008; Lee and Noppeney, 2011; Pekkola et al., 2005)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Visual cortices can send signals to auditory regions that can be exploited to establish coarse-grained acoustic representations.
claims.source: for example by receiving signals from visual cortices that can be exploited to establish coarse-grained acoustic representations (Bourguignon et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: Most studies focused on mapping activations rather than specific semantic or lexical speech content.
claims.source: This is in part because most studies focused on mapping activations rather than specific semantic or lexical speech content.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the methodological approach of previous studies.

claims.claim: Alternative accounts have been proposed which hold that visual and auditory speech representations are largely distinct.
claims.source: Indeed, alternative accounts have been proposed, which hold that visual and auditory speech representations are largely distinct (Bernstein and Liebenthal, 2014; Evans et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: It is important to distinguish purely stimulus driven neural activity from activity specifically representing a stimulus and contributing to the participant's percept on an individual trial.
claims.source: When investigating how speech is encoded in the brain, it is important to distinguish purely stimulus driven neural activity (e.g. classic 'activation') from activity specifically representing a stimulus and contributing to the participant's percept on an individual trial (Bouton et al., 2018; Grootswagers et al., 2018; Keitel et al., 2018; Panzeri et al., 2017; Tsunada et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous methodological studies.

claims.claim: Cerebral representations representing the physical speech are partly distinct from those reflecting the actually perceived meaning.
claims.source: Recent neuroimaging studies have suggested that those cerebral representations representing the physical speech are partly distinct from those reflecting the actually perceived meaning.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the context of recent neuroimaging studies.

claims.claim: Syllable identity can be decoded from temporal, occipital and frontal areas, but only focal activity in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) mediates perceptual categorisation.
claims.source: For example, syllable identity can be decoded from temporal, occipital and frontal areas, but only focal activity in the inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) mediates perceptual categorisation (Bouton et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: The encoding of the acoustic speech envelope is seen widespread in the brain, but correct word comprehension correlates only with focal activity in temporal and motor regions.
claims.source: Similarly, the encoding of the acoustic speech envelope is seen widespread in the brain, but correct word comprehension correlates only with focal activity in temporal and motor regions (Scott, 2019; Keitel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Activity in lower sensory pathways seems to correlate more with the actual physical stimulus, while activity in specific higher-tier regions correlates with the subjective percept.
claims.source: In general, activity in lower sensory pathways seems to correlate more with the actual physical stimulus, while activity in specific higher-tier regions correlates with the subjective percept (Crochet et al., 2019; Romo et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Participants performed a comprehension task based on individual sentences that were presented either acoustically or visually (lip reading), while brain activity was recorded using MEG.
claims.source: To this end, we exploited a paradigm in which participants performed a comprehension task based on individual sentences that were presented either acoustically or visually (lip reading), while brain activity was recorded using MEG (Keitel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claims.claim: Participants perceived the correct target word in approximately 70% of trials across auditory and visual conditions.
claims.source: On average, participants perceived the correct target word in approximately 70% of trials across auditory and visual conditions (chance level was 25%).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claims.claim: The behavioural performance did not differ significantly between auditory and visual conditions.
claims.source: The behavioural performance did not differ significantly between these conditions (Mauditory = 69.7%, SD = 7.1%, Mvisual = 71.7%, SD = 20.0%; t(19) = −0.42, p=0.68; Figure 1)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claims.claim: The addition of acoustic background noise equalised performance between auditory and visual conditions.
claims.source: demonstrating that the addition of acoustic background noise indeed equalised performance between conditions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral results.

claims.claim: The between-subject variability in performance was larger in the visual condition (between 31.7% and 98.3%).
claims.source: Still, the between-subject variability in performance was larger in the visual condition (between 31.7% and 98.3%), in line with the notion that lip reading abilities vary considerably across individuals (Bernstein and Liebenthal, 2014; Summerfield, 1992; Tye-Murray et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment, supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Participants' behavioural responses were influenced by both semantic and phonological features in both conditions.
claims.source: An explorative representational similarity analysis (RSA) (Evans and Davis, 2015; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008) indicated that participants' behavioural responses were influenced by both semantic and phonological features in both conditions (see Materials and methods, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the representational similarity analysis.

claims.claim: In both conditions phonological features influenced behaviour stronger than semantic features.
claims.source: A post-hoc comparison revealed that in both conditions phonological features influenced behaviour stronger than semantic features (Wilcoxon Signed-ranks test; Zauditory = 151, p=0.037, Zvisual = 189, p=0.002).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the representational similarity analysis.

claims.claim: Auditory speech was represented bilaterally in fronto-temporal areas, extending into intra-parietal regions within the left hemisphere.
claims.source: Auditory speech was represented bilaterally in fronto-temporal areas, extending into intra-parietal regions within the left hemisphere (Figure 2A; Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the MEG source activity classification analysis, shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Visual speech was represented bilaterally in occipital areas, as well as in left parietal and frontal areas.
claims.source: Visual speech was represented bilaterally in occipital areas, as well as in left parietal and frontal areas (Figure 2B), with classification performance between 25.9% and 33.9%.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the MEG source activity classification analysis, shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The regions representing word identity in both visual and auditory conditions overlapped in the middle and inferior temporal gyrus, the postcentral and supramarginal gyri, and the left inferior frontal gyrus.
claims.source: The regions representing word identity in both visual and auditory conditions overlapped in the middle and inferior temporal gyrus, the postcentral and supramarginal gyri, and the left inferior frontal gyrus (Figure 2C; overlap in green).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the MEG source activity classification analysis, shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Both auditory clusters and the occipital visual cluster contained grid points with substantial or strong evidence for a significant modality difference.
claims.source: However, both auditory clusters and the occipital visual cluster contained grid points with substantial or strong (bf10 > 3 and bf10 > 10, respectively) evidence for a significant modality difference.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis comparing auditory and visual word classification.

claims.claim: The visual postcentral region (POST), the IFG and the overlap region contained many grid points with substantial evidence for no difference between modalities.
claims.source: In contrast, the visual postcentral region (POST), the IFG and the overlap region contained many grid points with substantial evidence for no difference between modalities (1∕10 < bf10<1∕3).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis comparing auditory and visual word classification.

claims.claim: Auditory classification was significantly better in clusters covering left and right auditory cortices.
claims.source: Auditory classification was significantly better in clusters covering left and right auditory cortices, while visual classification was significantly better in bilateral visual sensory areas.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the full-brain cluster-based permutation test for modality difference.

claims.claim: Visual classification was significantly better in bilateral visual sensory areas.
claims.source: Auditory classification was significantly better in clusters covering left and right auditory cortices, while visual classification was significantly better in bilateral visual sensory areas.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the full-brain cluster-based permutation test for modality difference.

claims.claim: There was evidence for a statistically significant lateralisation for both auditory clusters.
claims.source: We found evidence for a statistically significant lateralisation for both auditory clusters (left cluster peaking in POST: t(17) = 5.15, pFDR <0.001; right cluster peaking in RO: t(17) = 4.26, pFDR <0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the lateralisation test.

claims.claim: In the auditory condition, five distinct clusters showed neural representations of word identity predictive of behaviour.
claims.source: In the auditory condition, we found five distinct clusters. Three were in the left hemisphere, peaking in the left inferior temporal gyrus (left ITG; Tsum = 469.55, p<0.001), the inferior frontal gyrus (left IFG; Tsum = 138.70, p<0.001), and the middle occipital gyrus (left MOG; Tsum = 58.44, p<0.001). In the right hemisphere, the two significant clusters were in the supplementary motor area (right SMA; Tsum = 312.48, p<0.001) and in the angular gyrus (right AG; Tsum = 68.59, p<0.001; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neurobehavioral analysis, shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: In the visual condition, four clusters showed neural representations of word identity predictive of behaviour.
claims.source: In the visual condition, we found four clusters: A left-hemispheric cluster in the inferior frontal gyrus (left IFG; Tsum = 144.15, p<0.001) and three clusters with right-hemispheric peaks, in the superior temporal gyrus (right STG; Tsum = 168.68, p<0.001), the superior frontal gyrus (right SFG; Tsum = 158.39, p<0.001) and the angular gyrus (right AG; Tsum = 37.42, p<0.001; Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neurobehavioral analysis, shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Perception-relevant auditory and visual representations did not overlap.
claims.source: Interestingly, these perception-relevant (i.e. predictive) auditory and visual representations did not overlap (Figure 3C), although some of them occurred in adjacent regions in the IFG and AG.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the neurobehavioral analysis, shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Three auditory clusters contained grid points that differed substantially or strongly between modalities (left ITG, left MOG, and right AG).
claims.source: Three auditory clusters contained grid points that differed substantially or strongly (bf10 > 3 and bf10 > 10, respectively) between modalities (left ITG, left MOG, and right AG).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of neurobehavioral prediction.

claims.claim: In two regions the majority of grid points provided substantial evidence for no difference between modalities (IFG and AG from the visual condition).
claims.source: In addition, in two regions the majority of grid points provided substantial evidence for no difference between modalities (IFG and AG from the visual condition).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of neurobehavioral prediction.

claims.claim: There was evidence for a significant modality specialisation for auditory words in four clusters in the left middle occipital gyrus, left calcarine gyrus, right posterior angular gyrus, and bilateral supplementary motor area.
claims.source: A separate full-brain cluster-based permutation test (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) provided evidence for a significant modality specialisation for auditory words in four clusters in the left middle occipital gyrus, left calcarine gyrus, right posterior angular gyrus, and bilateral supplementary motor area.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the full-brain cluster-based permutation test for modality difference in neurobehavioral prediction.

claims.claim: Regions predictive of visual word comprehension did not show a significant modality preference.
claims.source: On the other hand, regions predictive of visual word comprehension did not show a significant modality preference.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the full-brain cluster-based permutation test for modality difference in neurobehavioral prediction.

claims.claim: No evidence was found for significant cross-classification between auditory and visual conditions at the whole-brain level.
claims.source: At the whole-brain level, we found no evidence for significant cross-classification (two-sided cluster-based permutation statistics, neither at a corrected p=0.001 nor a more lenient p=0.05; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cross-decoding analysis.

claims.claim: Most grid points contained substantial evidence for no cross-classification between the auditory and visual conditions.
claims.source: An analysis of the Bayes factors for this cross-classification test confirmed that most grid points contained substantial evidence for no cross-classification between the auditory and visual conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, left panel).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of cross-classification.

claims.claim: There was strong evidence for significant cross-classification between the uni- and multisensory conditions in temporal and occipital regions.
claims.source: On the other hand, there was strong evidence for significant cross-classification between the uni- and multisensory conditions in temporal and occipital regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B, right panel).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of cross-classification.

claims.claim: Brain regions in which sensory representations shape speech comprehension are mostly distinct from those allowing the best prediction of the actual stimulus.
claims.source: The above results suggest that the brain regions in which sensory representations shape speech comprehension are mostly distinct from those allowing the best prediction of the actual stimulus (see Figure 4 for direct visualisation of the results from both analyses).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing stimulus classification and neurobehavioral prediction results.

claims.claim: Only parts of the left inferior temporal gyrus (auditory condition), the right superior temporal gyrus (visual condition) and the left inferior frontal gyrus (both conditions) feature high stimulus classification and a driving role for comprehension.
claims.source: Only parts of the left inferior temporal gyrus (auditory condition), the right superior temporal gyrus (visual condition) and the left inferior frontal gyrus (both conditions) feature high stimulus classification and a driving role for comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is a result from comparing stimulus classification and neurobehavioral prediction.

claims.claim: The accuracy by which local activity reflects the physical stimulus is generally not predictive of the impact of this local word representation on behaviour.
claims.source: In other words, the accuracy by which local activity reflects the physical stimulus is generally not predictive of the impact of this local word representation on behaviour.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the regression analysis between stimulus classification and neurobehavioral weights.

claims.claim: Group-level statistics of the participant-specific beta values provided no support for a consistent relationship between overall stimulus classification performance and the perceptual weight of each local representation across all grid points.
claims.source: Group-level statistics of the participant-specific beta values provided no support for a consistent relationship between these (auditory condition: b = 0.05 ± 0.11 [M ± SEM], t(17) = 0.50, pFDR = 0.81; visual condition: b = 0.03 ± 0.11 [M ± SEM], t(14) = 0.25, pFDR = 0.81; participant-specific regression slopes are depicted in Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the regression analysis between stimulus classification and neurobehavioral weights.

claims.claim: Stimulus classification performance was not significantly correlated with behavioural performance across participants.
claims.source: We found no significant clusters (all ps > 0.11, two-sided cluster-based permutation statistics, uncorrected across the four tests), indicating that stimulus classification performance was not significantly correlated with behavioural performance across participants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis between stimulus classification and behavioral performance.

claims.claim: In the large majority of brain regions, there is substantial evidence for no correlation between stimulus classification performance and behavioral performance.
claims.source: The corresponding Bayes factors confirm that in the large majority of brain regions, there is substantial evidence for no correlation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the Bayes factor analysis of correlations between stimulus classification and behavioral performance.

claims.claim: The cerebral representations of auditory and visual speech are mediated by both modality-specific and overlapping (potentially amodal) representations.
claims.source: Our results show that the cerebral representations of auditory and visual speech are mediated by both modality-specific and overlapping (potentially amodal) representations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Several parietal, temporal and frontal regions were engaged in the encoding of both acoustically and visually conveyed word identities.
claims.source: While several parietal, temporal and frontal regions were engaged in the encoding of both acoustically and visually conveyed word identities ('stimulus classification'), comprehension in both sensory modalities was driven mostly by distinct networks.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stimulus classification results.

claims.claim: Comprehension in both sensory modalities was driven mostly by distinct networks.
claims.source: While several parietal, temporal and frontal regions were engaged in the encoding of both acoustically and visually conveyed word identities ('stimulus classification'), comprehension in both sensory modalities was driven mostly by distinct networks.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claims.claim: Only the inferior frontal and anterior angular gyrus contained adjacent regions that contributed to both auditory and visual comprehension.
claims.source: Only the inferior frontal and anterior angular gyrus contained adjacent regions that contributed to both auditory and visual comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claims.claim: Auditory and visual cortices represent strongly modality-specific word identities.
claims.source: On the other hand, auditory and visual cortices represent strongly modality-specific word identities.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stimulus classification results.

claims.claim: Anterior angular and inferior frontal regions facilitate both auditory and visual comprehension.
claims.source: Second, it is also supported by the observation that anterior angular and inferior frontal regions facilitate both auditory and visual comprehension, while distinct regions support modality-specific comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claims.claim: Middle occipital and posterior angular representations specifically drive auditory comprehension.
claims.source: In particular, our data suggest that middle occipital and posterior angular representations specifically drive auditory comprehension.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claims.claim: Superior frontal and temporal regions are engaged in lip reading.
claims.source: In addition, superior frontal and temporal regions are engaged in lip reading, although we did not find strong evidence for a modality preference of these regions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the neurobehavioral prediction results.

claims.claim: None of the comprehension-relevant regions was strictly lateralised.
claims.source: None of these comprehension-relevant regions was strictly lateralised, in line with the notion that speech comprehension is largely a bilateral process (Kennedy-Higgins et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the lateralisation test, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The inability to cross-classify auditory and visual speech from local activity supports the conclusion that the nature of local representations of acoustic and visual speech is relatively distinct.
claims.source: The inability to cross-classify auditory and visual speech from local activity further supports the conclusion that the nature of local representations of acoustic and visual speech is relatively distinct.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cross-classification results.

claims.claim: Local activity could encode a given word based on acoustic or visual evidence but using distinct activity patterns.
claims.source: It could be that local activity encodes a given word based on acoustic or visual evidence but using distinct activity patterns.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cross-classification results.

claims.claim: The activity patterns by which auditory and visual speech are encoded may be partly distinct, even within regions that represent both acoustically and visually mediated word information.
claims.source: Our results hence provide evidence that the activity patterns by which auditory and visual speech are encoded may be partly distinct, even within regions that represent both acoustically and visually mediated word information, such as the inferior frontal and anterior angular gyrus.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cross-classification results.

claims.claim: The stimulus-domain classifier used may also capture processes potentially related to attention or motor preparation.
claims.source: This suggests that the stimulus-domain classifier used here may also capture processes potentially related to attention or motor preparation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the widespread classification results.

claims.claim: The segregation of comprehension-relevant auditory and visual representations provides a possible explanation for the finding that auditory or verbal skills and visual lip reading are uncorrelated in normal-hearing adults.
claims.source: The segregation of comprehension-relevant auditory and visual representations provides a possible explanation for the finding that auditory or verbal skills and visual lip reading are uncorrelated in normal-hearing adults (Jeffers and Barley, 1980; Mohammed et al., 2006; Summerfield, 1992).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claims.claim: Individual differences in lip reading represent something other than normal variation in speech perceptual abilities.
claims.source: Indeed, it has been suggested that individual differences in lip reading represent something other than normal variation in speech perceptual abilities (Summerfield, 1992).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Lip reading skills are unrelated to reading abilities in the typical adult population.
claims.source: For example, lip reading skills are unrelated to reading abilities in the typical adult population (Arnold and Köpsel, 1996; Mohammed et al., 2006), although a relationship is sometimes found in deaf or dyslexic children (Arnold and Köpsel, 1996; de Gelder and Vroomen, 1998; Kyle et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Visual speech may activate many regions in an unspecific manner, without engaging specific semantic or lexical representations, maybe as a result of attentional engagement or feed-back.
claims.source: Hence, it could be that visual speech may activate many regions in an unspecific manner, without engaging specific semantic or lexical representations, maybe as a result of attentional engagement or feed-back (Balk et al., 2013; Ozker et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claims.claim: Auditory cortical areas are equally activated by visual words and pseudo-words.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Studies demonstrate cross-modal activations in early sensory regions also for simplistic stimuli.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Visual speech comprehension is mediated by parietal and inferior frontal regions that likely contribute to both auditory and visual speech comprehension, but also engage superior temporal and superior frontal regions.
claims.source: Our results suggest that visual speech comprehension is mediated by parietal and inferior frontal regions that likely contribute to both auditory and visual speech comprehension, but also engage superior temporal and superior frontal regions.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claims.claim: The results support a route of visual speech into auditory cortical and temporal regions.

claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, contrasted with a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The results provide no evidence for an overlap of speech representations in the temporal lobe that would facilitate both lip-reading and acoustic speech comprehension.
claims.source: Thereby our results support a route of visual speech into auditory cortical and temporal regions but provide no evidence for an overlap of speech representations in the temporal lobe that would facilitate both lip-reading and acoustic speech comprehension, in contrast to recent suggestions from a lesion-based approach (Hickok et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, contrasted with a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The IFG and the anterior angular gyrus facilitate both auditory and visual speech comprehension.
claims.source: Our results suggest that these facilitate both auditory and visual speech comprehension, in line with previous suggestions (Simanova et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Previous work has implicated the IFG and anterior angular gyrus in the visual facilitation of auditory speech-in-noise perception and lip-reading itself.
claims.source: Previous work has also implicated these regions in the visual facilitation of auditory speech-in-noise perception (Giordano et al., 2017) and lip-reading itself (Bourguignon et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Lip-reading drives the improvement of speech perception in noise.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The representations of visual speech in the IFG and anterior angular gyrus may be central for hearing in noisy environments.
claims.source: hence suggesting that the representations of visual speech in these regions may be central for hearing in noisy environments.

claims.claim: The IFG and anterior angular gyrus in the present study resemble the left-lateralised dorsal pathway activated in deaf signers when seeing signed verbs.
claims.source: Interestingly, these regions resemble the left-lateralised dorsal pathway activated in deaf signers when seeing signed verbs (Emmorey et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Acoustic comprehension was related to occipital brain activity.

claims.claim: Salient sounds activate visual cortices.

claims.claim: Top-down projections provide visual regions with semantic information, for example about object categories.
claims.source: with top-down projections providing visual regions with semantic information, for example about object categories (Petro et al., 2017; Revina et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Attention may have automatically facilitated the entrance of top-down semantic information into occipital regions that, in a multisensory context, would encode the lip-movement trajectory.
claims.source: Attention may therefore have automatically facilitated the entrance of top-down semantic information into occipital regions that, in a multisensory context, would encode the lip-movement trajectory, in order to maximise task performance (McDonald et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The lack of significant cross-classification performance suggests that the nature of the top-down induced representation differs from that induced by direct lip-movement information.
claims.source: The lack of significant cross-classification performance suggests that the nature of this top-down induced representation differs from that induced by direct lip-movement information.

claims.claim: At the single neuron level some studies have proposed that only those neurons encoding the specific stimulus optimally are driving behaviour.

claims.claim: Brain regions allowing for a sub-optimal read-out of the actual stimulus are predictive of the perceptual outcome, whereas those areas allowing the best read-out not necessarily predict behaviour.

claims.claim: This dissociation between stimulus encoding and behavioral prediction is emerging in several recent studies on the neural basis underlying perception.

results.result: The study employed an MEG-based experimental design where 18 participants (after exclusions) performed a 4-alternative forced-choice word comprehension task on sentences presented either acoustically (with background noise) or visually (lip reading). Behavioral performance was approximately 70% correct in both conditions with no significant difference between modalities, though visual performance showed greater inter-individual variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C28 and C101-C108 collectively describe a well-designed experiment with appropriate controls (noise added to equalize performance), adequate sample size (n=18 for MEG), and clear behavioral outcomes. The statistical comparison (t(19)=-0.42, p=0.68) appropriately demonstrates no performance difference between conditions, validating the experimental manipulation.

results.result: Representational similarity analysis revealed that participants' behavioral responses were influenced by both semantic and phonological features in both auditory and visual conditions, with phonological features showing stronger influence than semantic features in both modalities.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 report results from an exploratory RSA analysis with appropriate statistical testing (repeated-measures ANOVA and post-hoc Wilcoxon tests). However, the authors acknowledge the limited number of word identities (n=9 in two categories) precludes strong conclusions about the relationship between these features and brain activity.

results.result: Multivariate classification of MEG source activity revealed that auditory speech was represented bilaterally in fronto-temporal areas (with significant lateralization), while visual speech was represented in bilateral occipital areas and left parietal/frontal regions. Regions representing word identity overlapped in middle/inferior temporal gyrus, postcentral/supramarginal gyri, and left inferior frontal gyrus, though Bayes factor analysis showed substantial evidence for modality differences in sensory cortices and evidence for no difference in some overlap regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C38 describe stimulus classification results using appropriate methods (LCMV beamformer, searchlight analysis, cluster-based permutation testing at p<0.001 FWE). The combination of frequentist and Bayesian statistics strengthens the conclusions. Classification performance (~10% above chance) is consistent with similar neuroimaging studies. The lateralization analysis provides additional rigor.

results.result: Neurobehavioral analysis revealed that auditory comprehension was driven by five distinct clusters (left ITG, IFG, MOG, right SMA, right AG) while visual comprehension was driven by four clusters (left IFG, right STG, SFG, AG). Critically, these perception-relevant representations did not overlap, though some occurred in adjacent regions in IFG and AG. Bayes factor analysis showed substantial evidence for modality specialization in auditory-predictive regions but not in visual-predictive regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C45 describe neurobehavioral prediction results using regularized logistic regression linking single-trial neural representations to behavior. The analysis is methodologically sound with appropriate corrections (p<0.05 FWE). The lack of overlap between auditory and visual comprehension-relevant regions is a key finding, though the authors appropriately note this analysis is primarily driven by correctly encoded trials due to the 4-AFC design.

results.result: Cross-classification analysis found no evidence for significant cross-classification between auditory and visual conditions at the whole-brain level, with Bayes factors providing substantial evidence for no cross-classification. However, significant cross-classification was found between unisensory and multisensory (audiovisual) conditions in temporal and occipital regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 report cross-decoding results using appropriate statistical methods. The negative result (no cross-classification between auditory and visual) is strengthened by Bayes factor analysis showing evidence for the null hypothesis. The positive control (successful cross-classification with audiovisual condition) demonstrates the method can detect cross-modal representations when present.

results.result: Brain regions where sensory representations shape speech comprehension are mostly distinct from those allowing best prediction of the actual stimulus. Only limited regions (parts of left ITG for auditory, right STG for visual, and left IFG for both) showed both high stimulus classification and a driving role for comprehension. Regression analysis found no consistent relationship between stimulus classification performance and neurobehavioral weights across all grid points.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 describe a critical dissociation between stimulus encoding and behavioral relevance, supported by within-participant robust regression analysis. The statistical results (auditory: b=0.05±0.11, t(17)=0.50, pFDR=0.81; visual: b=0.03±0.11, t(14)=0.25, pFDR=0.81) and Bayes factors (bf10=0.27 for both) provide strong evidence for no consistent relationship. This is a key conceptual finding of the paper.

results.result: Stimulus classification performance was not significantly correlated with behavioral performance across participants, with Bayes factors confirming substantial evidence for no correlation in the large majority of brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 report negative correlation results (all ps>0.11) strengthened by Bayes factor analysis. This finding complements the within-participant regression analysis and supports the conclusion that strong stimulus encoding does not necessarily predict behavioral performance.

results.result: The cerebral representations of auditory and visual speech are mediated by both modality-specific and overlapping representations. While several parietal, temporal, and frontal regions encoded both acoustically and visually conveyed word identities, comprehension in both modalities was driven mostly by distinct networks. Only the inferior frontal and anterior angular gyrus contained adjacent regions contributing to both auditory and visual comprehension, suggesting cerebral representations encoding word identities may be more modality-specific than often upheld.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C55-C60 represent the main conclusions of the paper, synthesizing results from stimulus classification and neurobehavioral analyses. These conclusions are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple analyses (classification, neurobehavioral prediction, cross-decoding, Bayes factors). The distinction between stimulus-driven and comprehension-relevant representations is a key conceptual advance.

results.result: Middle occipital and posterior angular representations specifically drive auditory comprehension, while superior frontal and temporal regions are engaged in lip reading (though without strong evidence for modality preference). None of the comprehension-relevant regions was strictly lateralized.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 describe specific regional findings from the neurobehavioral analysis. The lateralization analysis (all pFDR≥0.15) appropriately shows no strict lateralization. The finding of occipital involvement in auditory comprehension is unexpected but supported by the data and discussed in relation to top-down attention mechanisms.

results.result: The inability to cross-classify auditory and visual speech from local activity supports the conclusion that the nature of local representations of acoustic and visual speech is relatively distinct. The activity patterns by which auditory and visual speech are encoded may be partly distinct, even within regions that represent both acoustically and visually mediated word information.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 draw appropriate inferences from the cross-classification results. The interpretation that local activity could encode words using distinct activity patterns for different modalities is reasonable, though C65 is appropriately marked as speculative. The conclusion is strengthened by the Bayes factor evidence for no cross-classification.

results.result: The segregation of comprehension-relevant auditory and visual representations provides a possible neural explanation for the behavioral finding that auditory/verbal skills and visual lip reading are uncorrelated in normal-hearing adults, and that lip reading skills are unrelated to reading abilities in the typical adult population.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 connect the neural findings to established behavioral literature (cited appropriately). The neural dissociation observed in the study provides a plausible mechanistic explanation for the behavioral dissociations reported in prior work. However, this remains an inference rather than a direct demonstration of the link.

results.result: Visual speech comprehension is mediated by parietal and inferior frontal regions that likely contribute to both auditory and visual speech comprehension, but also engage superior temporal and superior frontal regions. The results support a route of visual speech into auditory cortical and temporal regions but provide no evidence for an overlap of speech representations in the temporal lobe that would facilitate both lip-reading and acoustic speech comprehension.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 synthesize findings about visual speech processing. The conclusions are supported by the neurobehavioral analysis showing IFG and anterior angular gyrus involvement in both modalities. The contrast with Hickok et al. (2018) is appropriate, though the authors acknowledge their results cannot directly address multisensory integration.

results.result: Acoustic comprehension was related to occipital brain activity. This unexpected finding is interpreted as potentially reflecting top-down semantic information entering occipital regions that would encode lip-movement trajectories in multisensory contexts, facilitated by attention to maximize task performance. The lack of cross-classification suggests this top-down representation differs from that induced by direct lip-movement information.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 describe an unexpected finding (occipital activity during auditory comprehension) with a speculative interpretation. While C82 is supported by the data (Figure 3), the mechanistic explanation in C85 is explicitly speculative and supported only by citations to related work. The inference in C86 is reasonable but indirect. This interpretation requires further validation.

results.result: Brain regions allowing sub-optimal read-out of the actual stimulus are predictive of perceptual outcome, whereas areas allowing the best read-out do not necessarily predict behavior. This dissociation between stimulus encoding and behavioral prediction is emerging in several recent studies and suggests that networks mediating speech comprehension cannot be understood by mapping speech representations during passive perception or task performance without analysis geared toward revealing perception-relevant representations.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C92 articulate a key conceptual contribution of the paper, supported by the dissociation between stimulus classification and neurobehavioral prediction results. The conclusion is strengthened by citations to converging evidence from other recent studies. This represents an important methodological and conceptual advance for the field.

results.result: Classification performance was highly significant and reached about 10% above chance level, consistent with other neuroimaging studies. By design, the neurobehavioral analysis was primarily driven by trials in which brain activity encoded the sensory stimulus correctly.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 acknowledge important methodological considerations. C93 appropriately contextualizes the classification performance with citations. C94 transparently acknowledges a limitation of the 4-AFC design - the analysis cannot specifically link incorrect stimulus encoding with behavior. This is an important caveat for interpreting the neurobehavioral results.

results.result: The specific task imposed may shape the behavioral relevance of local sensory representations. Studies showing perceptual relevance of optimally encoding neurons used tasks dependent on low-level features, while studies showing behavioral relevance of high-level regions relied on high-level information. This suggests that discussion of relevant networks underlying speech perception should always be task-focused, with predictions that changing task demands would shift the perceptual relevance of different brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C100 discuss task-dependence of neural representations, supported by appropriate citations. While C98-C99 are speculative predictions, they are reasonable extrapolations from the current findings and cited literature. The conclusion in C100 is an important conceptual point about interpreting neural mechanisms of perception.

results.result: MEG source reconstruction was performed using standard methods (LCMV beamformer, 6mm grid spacing, 6490 cortical grid points). Multivariate classification used spatial searchlights (1.2cm radius, typically 31 neighbors) on 500ms windows of activity following target word onset, rebinned at 20ms resolution. A correlation-based nearest-neighbor classifier was selected after testing multiple classifiers, with linear classifiers chosen for interpretability.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C119 describe the methodological pipeline with appropriate detail and citations. The choice of parameters (spatial smoothing, temporal binning, searchlight size, classifier type) is justified by testing alternatives and citing relevant literature. The methods are standard for MEG source analysis and multivariate classification.

results.result: Neurobehavioral analysis quantified the relationship between single-trial representational distances (within-target minus between-target correlations) and behavioral performance using regularized logistic regression. Phonological and semantic distances were computed using standard tools. Statistical analysis used cluster-based permutation testing with appropriate corrections (FWE p=0.001 for stimulus classification, p<0.05 for neurobehavioral analysis).
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125 describe the neurobehavioral analysis methods with appropriate detail and citations. The use of representational distance as a link between neural activity and behavior is well-established. The statistical methods (cluster-based permutation, FWE correction) are appropriate for the multiple comparisons problem in whole-brain analysis.

results.result: Visual speech carried by lip movements is an integral part of communication, yet it remains unclear to what extent visual and acoustic speech comprehension are mediated by the same brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 establish the background and motivation for the study. C1 is a well-established fact about communication. C2 accurately identifies a gap in current understanding that the study addresses. These claims appropriately frame the research question.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that visual speech provides redundant and complementary information to acoustic cues and enhances intelligibility in noise, yet behavioral studies show auditory and visual speech comprehension are uncorrelated with high inter-individual variability in lip reading. Neuroimaging studies have suggested convergence of acoustic and visual speech in specific brain regions, though alternative accounts propose largely distinct representations. Recent work emphasizes distinguishing stimulus-driven activity from activity contributing to perception.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C23 comprehensively review relevant prior literature with appropriate citations. The review accurately characterizes the tension between behavioral dissociation and proposed neural convergence, setting up the study's contribution. The emphasis on distinguishing stimulus encoding from perceptual relevance (C19-C23) establishes the methodological framework.

results.result: The widespread stimulus classification may capture processes related to attention or motor preparation rather than specific word representations. Visual speech may activate many regions unspecifically without engaging specific semantic or lexical representations, possibly due to attentional engagement or feedback.
results.evaluation: Claims C67 and C71 offer speculative interpretations of widespread activation patterns. While supported by citations to related work, these remain alternative explanations that are not directly tested in the current study. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than conclusions.

results.result: Previous work has implicated the IFG and anterior angular gyrus in visual facilitation of auditory speech-in-noise perception and lip-reading. Behavioral studies show lip-reading drives improvement of speech perception in noise, suggesting these regions may be central for hearing in noisy environments. These regions resemble the left-lateralized dorsal pathway activated in deaf signers viewing signed verbs.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81 connect the current findings to prior literature with appropriate citations. The inference in C80 about the role of these regions in noisy environments is reasonable given the cited behavioral work, though it extends beyond the current data. The comparison to sign language processing (C81) is interesting but remains speculative.

results.result: Prior studies show auditory cortical areas are equally activated by visual words and pseudo-words, and demonstrate cross-modal activations in early sensory regions for simplistic stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 cite relevant prior work supporting the interpretation that visual speech may activate auditory regions non-specifically. These citations appropriately support the discussion of why widespread activation may not reflect specific word representations.

results.result: At the single neuron level, some studies propose only optimally encoding neurons drive behavior, while others suggest sensory information and choice-predictive information can be decoupled across neurons. The intersection of brain activity predictive of stimulus and choice is difficult to quantify for high-dimensional data due to computational costs.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 review relevant theoretical and methodological literature with appropriate citations. These claims establish the conceptual framework for understanding the dissociation between stimulus encoding and behavioral prediction observed in the current study.
